overview: This file brings together U.S. and British economic-intelligence documents on Japan’s wartime iron, steel, and precision-engineering capabilities from 1940 to 1942. A naval attaché report describes shortages of alloying metals and high-quality special steel, rising raw-material costs, subsidies, and conflict between the Japanese Army and industrial interests; a Commerce Department memorandum assesses Japan’s dependence on imported scrap and pig iron while arguing that substantial stockpiles could sustain steel production after U.S. export restrictions; and a British Ministry of Economic Warfare study concludes that Japan could probably manufacture enough ball bearings for immediate military needs, although metallurgical and machine-tool weaknesses would impair their quality.

subfiles.title: Naval attaché report on scarcity of special steel in Japan
subfiles.from: H. H. Smith-Hutton, U.S. Naval Attaché, Tokyo
subfiles.to: U.S. Navy Department, Office of Naval Intelligence
subfiles.about: Reports shortages of high-quality special steel and alloying metals and the Japanese Army’s efforts to impose greater control over the steel industry.
subfiles.summary: The report attributes Japan’s special-steel difficulties to the European war, interrupted German and Swedish supplies, concern about possible American restrictions, and dwindling stocks of nickel, molybdenum, cobalt, and vanadium. Rising material prices made established military procurement prices untenable, leading the government to divert funds for large steel, coke, and coal subsidies rather than reconvene the Diet. It also describes conflict between the Army and the Commerce and Industry Ministry and plans to prioritize military producers, conserve scarce alloys, disseminate manufacturing expertise, and purge inefficient firms. Only five of eighty registered special-steel companies are rated first class, six are considered good, and sixty-nine are judged inferior.

subfiles.title: George Wythe’s informal transmittal of the Japanese steel memorandum
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Green, Chief, Division of Controls, Department of State
subfiles.about: Transmits informally a Commerce Department memorandum on raw materials for the Japanese steel industry.
subfiles.summary: Wythe forwards a copy of the Metals and Minerals Division memorandum entitled “Raw Material For The Japanese Steel Industry.” He explains that Assistant Director Carroll Wilson believed the analysis would interest Green and had asked that it be supplied informally.

subfiles.title: Raw Material for the Japanese Steel Industry
subfiles.from: J. Jos. W. Palmer, Assistant Chief, Metals and Minerals Division
subfiles.about: Quantitatively evaluates Japan’s supply of scrap, pig iron, and iron ore and the likely effect of U.S. restrictions on scrap exports.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum examines the effect of the October 1940 licensing restrictions that effectively ended U.S. scrap exports to Japan, using mostly 1934–1936 statistics because Japan had ceased publishing relevant figures after mid-1937. It reconstructs supplies from Japan, Korea, Manchuria, China, India, the Straits Settlements, and the United States, and estimates 1939 steel-ingot production at about six million tons. Palmer argues that imported American scrap was important but that Japan had probably accumulated between 1934 and 1939 at least 7.5 million tons of reserve pig iron and scrap, supplemented by material removed from occupied China. The memorandum concludes that these reserves, together with continuing supplies from Japan’s controlled territories, might sustain production at 1939 levels for at least one year and possibly two; tables compare world steel capacity and Japan’s raw-material balance in 1934–1936.

subfiles.title: London Embassy despatch transmitting memorandum on Japanese ball bearings
subfiles.from: James Somerville, for the Chargé d’Affaires ad interim, U.S. Embassy London
subfiles.to: The Secretary of State, Washington, D.C.
subfiles.about: Transmits a British Ministry of Economic Warfare assessment of Japan’s capacity to replace foreign ball-bearing supplies with domestic production.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy forwards an informal Enemy Resources Department memorandum on Japanese ball-bearing production. Somerville summarizes its conclusion that four known factories could produce the equivalent of 60,000 bearings of 30-mm bore daily, enough to meet probable Japanese wartime requirements in quantity but not necessarily in quality. He notes that currently satisfactory bearings in Japanese aircraft, tanks, and naval vessels probably came from prewar foreign stocks and that Japan had shown interest in obtaining German bearings through blockade running. The April 18 date follows the enclosure caption and the file’s terminal date; page 15’s OCR renders the day as April 14.

subfiles.title: Ministry of Economic Warfare memorandum on ball-bearing production in Japan
subfiles.from: Enemy Resources Department, Ministry of Economic Warfare
subfiles.about: Assesses the capacity, organization, technological limits, and probable product quality of Japan’s domestic ball-bearing industry.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum identifies four Japanese factories—Tokyo Bearing Seizo, Nihon Seiko, Fujikoshi Kozai, and Amatsuji—and estimates their combined capacity at the equivalent of 60,000 30-mm-bore bearings per day, compared with Germany’s estimated 220,000. It judges this probably sufficient for Japan’s quantitative military requirements, while emphasizing the challenges of producing high-carbon chromium steel, controlling heat treatment, forging large races, and performing precision grinding. Because specialized ball-grinding machines were difficult to obtain or copy and may all have been concentrated at Amatsuji, machinery could limit output. The authors expect domestically produced bearings, especially large ones, to be inferior to Swedish and other imported products, while explaining the quality of bearings already observed in Japanese weapons as the result of prewar foreign stockpiling.

interest: The file is especially useful because it juxtaposes three stages of Allied assessment: an immediate 1940 attaché warning about acute special-steel shortages, a more cautious statistical argument that Japan possessed large ferrous-material reserves, and a 1942 appraisal separating ball-bearing quantity from quality. It exposes both the sophistication and uncertainty of economic intelligence when Japanese statistics were unavailable, as analysts combined press reports, conversations, pre-1937 data, industrial estimates, and engineering judgments. The named-company rankings, factory-output estimates, stockpile calculations, and discussion of institutional conflict between the Army and industrialists provide unusually concrete evidence for studying Japanese mobilization, Allied economic warfare, and the anticipated effects of embargo and blockade.
